Provisional text
OPINION OF ADVOCATE GENERAL
RICHARD DE LA TOUR
delivered on 2 July 2026 ( 1 )
Case C ‑ 300/25 [Duftošek]  ( i )
SQ
v
YR
(Request for a preliminary ruling from the Nejvyšší soud (Supreme Court, Czech Republic))
( Reference for a preliminary ruling – Area of freedom, security and justice – Regulation (EU) 2016/1103 – Jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition and enforcement of decisions in matters of matrimonial property regimes – First sentence of Article 1(1) and Article 1(2)(g) – Article 3(1)(a) – Concept of ‘matrimonial property regimes’ – Spouses who have opted for the separate property regime – Immovable property acquired in co-ownership solely by those spouses during their marriage – Proceedings brought after divorce for the liquidation and division of that co-owned property )
I.       Introduction
1.         Spouses residing in the Czech Republic, who had opted for a contractual separate property regime, acquired, in co-ownership ( en indivision ), a property unit situated in France. Following their divorce, one of the spouses brought proceedings before a Czech court with a view to liquidating and dividing that co-owned property, on the basis of rules of Czech general law.
2.         The Nejvyšší soud (Supreme Court, Czech Republic), which is the referring court, must rule on the international jurisdiction of the court seised. It is uncertain of the extent to which the dispute’s connection with the marriage is significant when determining whether it falls within the scope of Regulation (EU) 2016/1103, ( 2 ) which defines the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’, or of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012, ( 3 ) since the spouses chose a matrimonial property regime that does not organise their property relationships and the existence of a co‑ownership arrangement ( indivision ) between them does not depend on the continuation of their matrimonial relationship.
3.         That request for an interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ arises in a novel context, having regard to the Court’s case-law in civil and commercial matters, which predates Regulation 2016/1103, applicable to matrimonial property regimes, and to the resulting choices of the EU legislature.
4.         Since matters relating to ‘the nature of rights in rem relating to a property’ ( 4 ) are excluded from the scope of Regulation 2016/1103 and the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated have exclusive jurisdiction in proceedings concerning rights in rem in immovable property under Article 24(1) of the Brussels I bis Regulation, and since the co‑ownership arrangement at issue is governed by such rights, the problem is immediately apparent. Clearly, two opposing forces of attraction are at work, namely that of the law governing the matrimonial property regime and that of the law governing rights in rem .
5.         This thus gives the Court an opportunity to define, with precision, what comes within the scope of property relationships between spouses in connection with the marriage or its dissolution in a very common factual setting, namely the acquisition of property in common by spouses who are subject to a separate property regime. The task is complex in so far as this definition must be coordinated with the definition derived from the Court’s case-law on rights in rem in immovable property which delineates the scope of the Brussels I bis Regulation and Regulation (EU) No 650/2012. ( 5 ) Moreover, particular care is required because of the impact that delimitation of the scope of Regulation 2016/1103 has on other types of co-ownership which may exist between (former) spouses depending, where appropriate, on when the co-ownership arrangement is liquidated (during the marriage or after its dissolution) and on the rights of third parties.
6.         Since the scope of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ must be examined in the light of its definition in Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103 and the exclusion set out in Article 1(2)(g) thereof, I shall set out the reasons why I am of the view that:
–        that concept encompasses the property relationships of the spouses organised under a co‑ownership arrangement which is not governed by the matrimonial property regime that they have chosen; and
–        the dispute relating to the liquidation and the division of co‑owned property does not concern the nature of rights in rem over that property, within the meaning of that regulation.
II.     Legal framework
A.       European Union Law
1.       The Brussels I   bis Regulation
7.         Article 1 of the Brussels I bis Regulation, which appears in Chapter I thereof, entitled ‘Scope and definitions’, provides:
‘1.      This Regulation shall apply in civil and commercial matters whatever the nature of the court or tribunal. …
2.      The Regulation shall not apply to:
(a)      the status or legal capacity of natural persons, rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship or out of a relationship deemed by the law applicable to such relationship to have comparable effects to marriage;
… ’
8.         Under the heading ‘Jurisdiction’, Chapter II of that regulation contains several sections, including Section 6, entitled ‘Exclusive jurisdiction’. The first subparagraph of Article 24(1) in that section is worded as follows:
‘The following courts of a Member State shall have exclusive jurisdiction, regardless of the domicile of the parties:
(1)      in proceedings which have as their object rights in rem in immovable property or tenancies of immovable property, the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated.’
2.       Regulation 2016/1103
9.         Recitals 15, 18 and 52 of Regulation 2016/1103 state:
‘(15)      To provide married couples with legal certainty as to their property and offer them a degree of predictability, all the rules applicable to matrimonial property regimes should be covered in a single instrument.
…
(18)      The scope of this Regulation should include all civil-law aspects of matrimonial property regimes, both the daily management of matrimonial property and the liquidation of the regime, in particular as a result of the couple’s separation or the death of one of the spouses. For the purposes of this Regulation, the term “matrimonial property regime” should be interpreted autonomously and should encompass not only rules from which the spouses may not derogate but also any optional rules to which the spouses may agree in accordance with the applicable law, as well as any default rules of the applicable law. It includes not only property arrangements specifically and exclusively envisaged by certain national legal systems in the case of marriage but also any property relationships, between the spouses and in their relations with third parties, resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, or the dissolution thereof.
…
(52)      The law determined as the law applicable to the matrimonial property regime should govern the matrimonial property regime from the classification of property of one or both spouses into different categories during the marriage and after its dissolution, to the liquidation of the property. It should include the effects of the matrimonial property regime on a legal relationship between a spouse and third parties. However, the law applicable to matrimonial property regime may be invoked by a spouse against a third party to govern such effects only when the legal relations between the spouse and the third party arose at a time where the third party knew or should have known of that law.’
10.       Article 1 of that regulation, entitled ‘Scope’, provides:
‘1.      This Regulation shall apply to matrimonial property regimes.
It shall not apply to revenue, customs or administrative matters.
2.      The following shall be excluded from the scope of this Regulation:
…
(c)      maintenance obligations;
(d)      the succession to the estate of a deceased spouse;
…
(f)      the entitlement to transfer or adjustment between spouses, in the case of divorce, legal separation or marriage annulment, of rights to retirement or disability pension accrued during marriage and which have not generated pension income during the marriage;
(g)      the nature of rights in rem relating to a property; and
(h)      any recording in a register of rights in immoveable or moveable property, including the legal requirements for such recording, and the effects of recording or failing to record such rights in a register.’
11.       Under the heading ‘Definitions’, Article 3 of that regulation provides, in paragraph 1 thereof:
‘For the purposes of this Regulation:
(a)      “matrimonial property regime” means a set of rules concerning the property relationships between the spouses and in their relations with third parties, as a result of marriage or its dissolution;
(b) “matrimonial property agreement” means any agreement between spouses or future spouses by which they organise their matrimonial property regime;
… ’
12.       Article 6 of that regulation, entitled ‘Jurisdiction in other cases’, provides, in paragraph (b) thereof:
‘Where no court of a Member State has jurisdiction pursuant to Article 4 or 5 or in cases other than those provided for in those Articles, jurisdiction to rule on a matter of the spouses’ matrimonial property regime shall lie with the courts of the Member State:
…
(b)      in whose territory the spouses were last habitually resident, in so far as one of them still resides there at the time the court is seised …’
13.       Article 21 of Regulation 2016/1103, entitled ‘Unity of the applicable law’, states:
‘The law applicable to a matrimonial property regime pursuant to Article 22 or 26 shall apply to all assets falling under that regime, regardless of where the assets are located.’
14.       Article 27 of that regulation, entitled ‘Scope of the applicable law’, provides:
‘The law applicable to the matrimonial property regime pursuant to this Regulation shall govern, inter alia:
(a)      the classification of property of either or both spouses into different categories during and after marriage;
(b)      the transfer of property from one category to the other one;
(c)      the responsibility of one spouse for liabilities and debts of the other spouse;
(d)      the powers, rights and obligations of either or both spouses with regard to property;
(e)      the dissolution of the matrimonial property regime and the partition, distribution or liquidation of the property;
(f)      the effects of the matrimonial property regime on a legal relationship between a spouse and third parties; and
(g)      the material validity of a matrimonial property agreement.’
B.       Czech law
15.       The zákon č. 89/2012 SB., občanský zákoník (Law No 89/2012 on the Civil Code) (‘the Civil Code’) provides, in Paragraph 708 thereof, that anything that belongs to spouses, has a property value, and is not excluded from legal relations, constitutes part of the community of property of the spouses. According to subparagraph 2 of Paragraph 708, that community of property is subject to a statutory regime, a contractual regime or a regime based on a court decision.
16.       Under Paragraph 709(1) of the Civil Code, in the statutory regime, community of property includes assets acquired by one of the spouses or both spouses jointly during the marriage, with the exception of the assets specified in that provision.
17.       The first sentence of Paragraph 716(1) of the Civil Code provides that spouses may agree on a matrimonial property regime that differs from the statutory regime.
18.       According to the first sentence of Paragraph 717(1) of that code, a contractual matrimonial regime may consist of a separate property regime.
19.       In accordance with Paragraph 729 of that code, in the separate property regime, a spouse may dispose freely of his or her property without the other spouse’s consent.
20.       Paragraph 1115(1) of the Civil Code provides that persons who hold title to property together are co-owners.
21.       Paragraph 1140 of that code provides that no person may be compelled to remain a co-owner and that each co-owner may at any time request that his or her share in a common property be severed, if the co-owned property can be divided, or that the co-ownership arrangement be terminated.
22.       According to Paragraph 1143 of that code, where co-owners do not agree on the termination of the co-ownership arrangement, the decision is to be made by a court at the request of one of the co-owners. If a court decides to terminate a co-ownership arrangement, it must also determine the arrangements for the division between the co-owners.
III.  The facts of the dispute in the main proceedings and the question referred for a preliminary ruling
23.       The applicant, SQ, and the defendant, YR, married on 1 May 2015 and decided to make their property relationships subject to a contractual separate property regime ( 6 ) and to Czech law.
24.       During their marriage, they acquired property ( 7 ) situated in Paris (France) in co-ownership, each of them thus being half-owners of the property, according to SQ. ( 8 ) In 2020, their marriage was dissolved. The spouses’ last habitual residence was in the Czech Republic. The dispute between the former spouses concerns the liquidation and division of the co-owned immovable property. ( 9 )
25.       By order of 26 October 2022, the Obvodní soud pro Prahu 5 (Prague 5 District Court, Czech Republic), ruling at first instance, held that the proceedings for the liquidation and division of that co‑owned property are governed by general law and therefore fall within the material scope of the Brussels I bis Regulation. In accordance with Article 24(1) of that regulation, it is the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated, in this case the French courts, that have jurisdiction to hear such proceedings.
26.       That decision was overturned by the Městský soud v Praze (Municipal Court, Prague, Czech Republic) on appeal by the applicant, SQ. According to that court, the case falls within the scope of Regulation 2016/1103 on the ground that the term ‘matrimonial property regime’, which is an autonomous concept of EU law, encompasses any optional rules that spouses may agree between themselves in accordance with the applicable law. Therefore, the separate property regime constitutes a matrimonial property regime within the meaning of that regulation in so far as it concerns property rights arising from marriage. Consequently, the Czech courts have international jurisdiction to hear that case on the basis of Article 6(b) of that regulation.
27.       The defendant, YR, brought an appeal on a point of law against that decision before the Nejvyšší soud (Supreme Court).
28.       That court states that the dispute relating to the liquidation and division of the immovable property held in co‑ownership between the former spouses is governed by general rules of national private law ( 10 ) and has no connection with the marriage or the law governing spouses’ property relationships, and that it is generally accepted that such proceedings fall within the scope of civil and commercial matters within the meaning of the Brussels I bis Regulation. In the case of co‑ownership of immovable property, the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated have exclusive jurisdiction, in accordance with Article 24(1) of that regulation.
29.       However, the referring court is questioning the significance, for the resolution of the dispute, of the existence of the marriage, and likewise of the fact that the co‑ownership arrangement exists solely between the (former) spouses and results from their choice of an agreed separate property regime.
30.       In that regard, it explains that, under Czech law, a co‑ownership arrangement between spouses who have opted for a separate property regime is not distinguished from other forms of co‑ownership also governed by general law, including as regards the grounds which may justify its liquidation, the arrangements for its division and the time frame within which these occur.
31.       It notes that the Court has not yet ruled on whether, in a situation such as that at issue in the present case, the dispute constitutes a specific property dispute between spouses arising directly from the matrimonial relationship or its dissolution ( 11 ) – and is therefore governed by the rules on matrimonial property regimes under Regulation 2016/1103 – or whether it is a property dispute between spouses under general law that is unrelated to their marriage, and is thus a civil or commercial matter, within the meaning of the Brussels I bis Regulation.
32.       In those circumstances, the Nejvyšší soud (Supreme Court) decided to stay the proceedings and to refer the following question to the Court of Justice for a preliminary ruling:
‘Do proceedings for the [liquidation and division] of joint ownership interests in an immoveable property, acquired by the spouses as joint ownership interests as a result of an agreed separate property regime, constitute proceedings on a matrimonial property regime within the meaning of Articles 1 and 3(1)(a), of [Regulation 2016/1103]?’
33.       SQ, YR, the Czech Government and the European Commission submitted written observations and participated in the hearing held on 16 April 2026, during which the parties responded to questions put to them by the Court for oral answer.
IV.     Analysis
34.       The question referred for a preliminary ruling seeks to determine the international jurisdiction of the Czech court seised, on the basis of Article 6 of Regulation 2016/1103 ( 12 ) in respect of an application for the liquidation ( 13 ) and division of an immovable property held in co‑ownership, purchased in France by spouses who are subject to a separate property regime. ( 14 ) That question relates to the scope of that regulation, ( 15 ) which means that it is necessary to clarify the scope of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’, as defined in Article 3(1)(a) of that regulation and as may be inferred from the exclusion in Article 1(2)(g) thereof.
35.       The criteria for defining that concept should be derived having regard to the limits imposed on the court at the stage at which international jurisdiction is determined. It is apparent from the Court’s case-law on EU regulations in civil and commercial matters that the court seised examines neither the admissibility nor the substance of the application, but identifies only those factors that, in the given legal situation and according to the law relied upon, are capable of providing a basis for its jurisdiction. ( 16 )
36.       I would point out that the account of the facts of the main proceedings, as supplemented at the hearing, ( 17 ) leads me from the outset to exclude from my analysis the notion of a ‘matrimonial property agreement’, within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of Regulation 2016/1103, since no agreement was concluded between the spouses to govern the co‑ownership arrangement between them in order to adapt the separate property regime they had chosen. ( 18 )
A.       Preliminary observations on the methodology for interpreting the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’
37.       It must first be noted, as several authors have done, ( 19 ) that the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ is used in most other EU regulations as a criterion for exclusion or delimitation, in particular in Article 1(2)(a) of the Brussels I bis Regulation, ( 20 ) Article 1(2)(c) of the Rome I Regulation, ( 21 ) Article 1(2)(b) of the Rome II Regulation ( 22 ) and Article 1(2)(d) of Regulation No 650/2012. The most precise provision is Article 1(2)(e) of the Rome III Regulation. ( 23 ) It provides that that regulation does not apply to the property consequences of the marriage. Consequently, it is possible to refer to the case-law and the commentaries on those articles in order to define the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’.
38.       Second, in the judgment of 1 March 2018, Mahnkopf , ( 24 ) the Court defined what makes it possible to distinguish the scope of two regulations relating to matters excluded from the Brussels I bis Regulation, namely succession and matrimonial property regimes. I therefore consider it important to make it clear from the outset that the request for interpretation submitted to the Court arises in a different context. The Brussels I bis Regulation, which forms the basis for cooperation in civil matters, ( 25 ) is applicable in all Member States. That is not the case for Regulation 2016/1103, which is binding only on 18 Member States in the framework of enhanced cooperation. ( 26 ) Consequently, the rules on jurisdiction and recognition of judgments, which are based on the principle of mutual trust, apply only between Member States bound by that regulation. A broad interpretation of the scope of that regulation would have the effect of restricting the scope of the Brussels I bis Regulation and would mean that the exclusive jurisdiction of the court of the Member State in which the immovable property concerned is situated no longer applies. The courts of States not bound by Regulation 2016/1103 must therefore apply their domestic rules in order to determine their international jurisdiction and to recognise the judgments given. I am of the view that those consequences should not affect the interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’. ( 27 ) I would add, in that regard, that it is necessary to take into consideration the fact that certain rules of jurisdiction are applicable in situations which concern states not bound by Regulation 2016/1103 ( 28 ) or third states ( 29 ) and that the rules concerning conflict of laws are also applicable in relations with states not bound by that regulation. ( 30 )
39.       Third, Chapter I of Regulation 2016/1103 comprises Articles 1 to 3, which are devoted to the delimitation of its scope and definitions, which marks a significant difference between that regulation and the Convention on the law applicable to matrimonial property regimes. ( 31 )
40.       Article 1 of that regulation, which defines, in the first sentence of paragraph 1, its scope ratione materiae relating to ‘matrimonial property regimes’, is presented in legal literature as being decisive for the interpretation of that regulation, since it sets out exhaustively the matters which are excluded. ( 32 ) Those not listed therein are considered to be included if they fall within the scope of that regulation. ( 33 )
41.       Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103 defines a ‘matrimonial property regime’ as ‘a set of rules concerning the property relationships between the spouses and in their relations with third parties, as a result of marriage or its dissolution’. ( 34 )
42.       Fourth, in recital 18 of that regulation, it is stated that:
–        ‘the term “matrimonial property regime” should be interpreted autonomously’;
–        it ‘should encompass not only rules from which the spouses may not derogate but also any optional rules to which the spouses may agree in accordance with the applicable law, as well as any default rules of the applicable law’, and
–        it ‘includes not only property arrangements specifically and exclusively envisaged by certain national legal systems in the case of marriage but also any property relationships, between the spouses and in their relations with third parties, resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, or the dissolution thereof’.
43.       Fifth, Article 3(1)(a) and recital 18 of Regulation 2016/1103 are in line with the Court’s case-law on the exclusion of matrimonial property regimes from the scope of European instruments in civil and commercial matters. They also cover spouses’ relations with third parties resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, or the dissolution thereof.
44.       Accordingly, that case-law must be recalled in order to determine how, in the particular circumstances of the case in the main proceedings, it may be used to interpret Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103 (B), before clarifying the implications of the framework laid down by that regulation, as regards both its scope (C) and the limitations it imposes in respect of rights in rem , in light of the subject matter of the issue to be addressed and the determination of the applicable law (D).
B.       The case-law prior to Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103
45.       The referring court rightly cites two judgments of the Court defining the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ in the context of exclusion from the scope of the Brussels Convention, in point 1 of the second paragraph of Article 1 thereof, ( 35 ) and from the scope of the Brussels I bis Regulation, in Article 1(2)(a) thereof.
46.       In the judgment in de Cavel , the Court held that ‘the term “rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship” includes not only property arrangements specifically and exclusively envisaged by certain national legal systems in the case of marriage but also any proprietary relationships resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, or the dissolution thereof; disputes relating to the assets of spouses in the course of proceedings for divorce [( 36 )] may therefore, depending on the circumstances, concern or be closely connected with: (1) questions relating to the status of persons; or (2) proprietary legal relationships between spouses resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship or the dissolution thereof; or (3) proprietary legal relations existing between them which have no connection with marriage[, and] whereas disputes of the latter category fall within the scope of the [Brussels] Convention, those relating to the first two categories must be excluded therefrom’. ( 37 )
47.       In the order in Iliev , the Court held, applying the second of those criteria, that a dispute between former spouses relating to the liquidation of movable property acquired during the marriage concerns proprietary legal relationships resulting directly from the dissolution of the marriage and therefore does not come within the scope of the Brussels I bis Regulation. ( 38 )
48.       In the first of the cases which gave rise to those decisions, the matters relating to the matrimonial property regime brought before the referring courts were connected with divorce proceedings. In the second, the dispute, which arose after the divorce, concerned whether or not a vehicle purchased and registered in the name of the wife, which was to be determined in accordance with specific rules of the Family Code on jointly acquired property, was common property for the purposes of liquidation. ( 39 )
49.       Since the criterion of property relationships between spouses resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship or the dissolution thereof is set out in Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103, it is necessary to consider whether the judgment in de Cavel   and the order in Iliev are applicable , by analogy , to the present case.
50.       The referring court has rightly noted that there are grounds to express some reservations in that regard.
51.       In the present case, the situation is different for two reasons. First, the dispute concerns immovable property held in common, and the common ownership of that property has no direct connection with the matrimonial property regime chosen, since the spouses opted for a separate property regime which, by definition, does not create any community of property. Second, the legal regime governing that property is a co-ownership regime governed by general law, applicable to all persons, whether married or not. ( 40 )
52.       I would add that, although the former spouses’ property relationship (the co‑ownership arrangement) arose during the marriage, it is difficult to regard it as resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, in view of the spouses’ choice, from the outset of their union, to keep their property separate. ( 41 ) In those circumstances, might the property relationships between the spouses then be unconnected with the marriage? Such a finding should lead one to refer to the third criterion set out in the judgment in de Cavel ,   ( 42 ) under which the dispute would not be excluded from the field of civil and commercial matters.
53.       Consequently, the Court is called upon to state whether the fact that that co‑ownership arrangement involves no one other than the spouses and is necessarily linked to their choice of a contractual separate property regime, which excludes any community of property, is sufficient to consider that that situation falls within the scope of Regulation 2016/1103.
54.       The answer to that question entails determining the extent to which the EU legislature drew inspiration from the Court’s case-law and adopted a broad interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ when defining it in that regulation.
C.       The concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ in the context of Regulation 2016/1103
55.       Several reasons, arising from the Court’s methods of interpretation, justify interpreting that concept broadly.
1.       The wording of Article 3 (1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103
56.       First, the definition of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ set out in that article must be read in the light of the judgment in de Cavel in which it is stated that it covers ‘any proprietary relationships resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship or the dissolution thereof’.   ( 43 ) That wording is inspired by the expression used in the Schlosser Report , namely ‘property rights arising from the matrimonial relationship’ .   ( 44 ) That report states that ‘the mutual rights of spouses arising from “matrimonial regimes” correspond largely with what are best described in English as “rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship”’. ( 45 )
57.       In that regard, reference is made to the difficulties posed by the concept of ‘rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship’ arising from the fact that the United Kingdom and Ireland have no equivalent legal concept. In principle, property rights as between spouses are governed by general law. ( 46 )
58.       It is also noted that the concept of ‘rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship’ does not cover the same legal relations in all the ‘original Member States’. ( 47 ) Professor Schlosser thus highlighted the existence of various types of non‑exclusive systems, whereby those states have been able to develop legal institutions specific to relations between spouses, the main feature of which is to provide a comprehensive, albeit not exclusive, set of rules governing property, which may be contractual or statutory and which is supplemented, where appropriate, by rules governing proprietary relationships applicable to all spouses irrespective of the specific rights in property arising out of a matrimonial relationship adopted. ( 48 )
59.       Those points drawn from the Schlosser Report on the diversity of legal systems, which are still relevant today, ( 49 ) seem to me to be essential. I take the view that the definition of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ covers property relationships between spouses that are governed by general law, and not only by a single comprehensive set of rules on matrimonial property.
60.       The Court has not yet had the opportunity to rule on that question, since it has so far given rulings in the light of circumstances falling within the scope of specific provisions governing property relationships between spouses, namely either protective measures adopted in divorce proceedings (the judgment in de Cavel ), or a dispute concerning whether the property acquired during the marriage formed part of the spouses’ common property ( the order in Iliev ).   ( 50 )
61.       Second, I note that, although recital 18 of Regulation 2016/1103 refers to all property relationships between spouses ‘resulting directly from the matrimonial relationship, or the dissolution thereof’, ( 51 ) that adverb does not appear in the definition of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ set out in Article 3(1)(a) of that regulation.
62.       Like Dirk Looschelders, ( 52 ) I am of the view that it must be inferred from the wording of that provision, which is analogous in various language versions, ( 53 ) that the mere fact that property relationships arise from the marriage or its dissolution is a sufficient criterion. It can therefore be accepted that the requirement of a direct connection, as stated in the judgment in de Cavel   and the order in Iliev   ( 54 ) no longer needs to be satisfied .
63.       In those circumstances, it is necessary to ensure that a broad interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’, based on the wording of Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103, is justified not only by that wording but also in the light of the objectives pursued by the EU legislature and the scheme and context of that regulation.
2.       The objectives pursued by Regulation 2016/1103, and the scheme and context thereof
64.       First, the EU legislature clearly expressed the intention to adopt an instrument to eliminate the difficulties experienced by couples in managing or dividing their property, ( 55 ) by bringing together in Regulation 2016/1103 all the rules applicable to matrimonial property regimes, rules consisting of provisions on jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition or, as the case may be, acceptance, enforceability and enforcement of decisions, authentic instruments and court settlements. ( 56 )
65.       Regulation 2016/1103 is based on the fundamental principle of unity: in principle, a single authority has jurisdiction to rule on all matters relating to the spouses’ property relationships; that authority is to apply a single law ( 57 ) chosen by the spouses ( 58 ) or determined according to the objective connecting factors set out in that regulation, ( 59 ) which may be invoked against third parties under certain conditions. ( 60 ) That law is applicable to all of the spouses’ assets, regardless of where the assets are located, ( 61 ) as well as to their debts.
66.       The aim of simplifying the spouses’ legal position is very clearly reflected in the consequences of that principle of unity for jurisdiction and the applicable law.
67.       Thus, as regards jurisdiction, in particular where the dispute concerns immovable property, the desire to preserve the unity of jurisdiction ( 62 ) and of the law applicable to all of their assets ( 63 ) has prevailed over the reasons justifying the jurisdiction of the courts of the Member State in which the immovable property is situated. That jurisdiction is described in Regulation 2016/1103 as subsidiary, ( 64 ) whereas, in the judgment of 17 December 2015, Komu and Others , ( 65 )   which concerns the interpretation of the first subparagraph of Article 22(1) of Regulation No 44/2001, ( 66 ) the Court held that an action for the termination of co-ownership in undivided shares of immovable property situated in Spain by way of sale, brought before a Finnish court by co-owners residing in Finland, ( 67 ) falls within the category of proceedings which have as their object rights in rem in immovable property, which comes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated, ( 68 ) relying primarily on considerations of sound administration of justice. ( 69 )
68.       As regards the law applicable to the property relationships of the couple, the immutability ( 70 ) of that law strengthens the principle of unity. Furthermore, as regards immovable property, it should be noted that there is no special connecting factor to the law of the country in which the property is situated for the purposes of governing the protection of the family home. ( 71 ) As is made clear in the second sentence of recital 53 of Regulation 2016/1103, the rules on the family home fall within the scope of that regulation. ( 72 ) Moreover, it is not permissible to provide for the application of different laws to certain assets or depending on the nature of those assets. ( 73 ) Finally, from a more general perspective, it should be noted that that regulation covers not only rules of an imperative nature but also any optional and default rules. ( 74 )
69.       Consequently, it appears that the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ within the meaning of Regulation 2016/1103 should encompass all the property consequences of marriage, in so far as they do not fall under a specific regime , such as, in particular, the regime governing maintenance obligations, that governing compensatory adjustment of pension rights ( 75 ) or the law applicable to the succession to the estate of a deceased spouse. ( 76 )
70.       Secondly, other arguments based on the scheme of Regulation 2016/1103 support the interpretation that the definition of the autonomous concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ in Article 3(1)(a) of that regulation is deliberately broad. They may be inferred from the relationship between that definition and Article 27 of that regulation, which governs the scope of the applicable law, ( 77 ) during the marriage and after its dissolution.
71.       According to Peter Mankowski, ( 78 ) Article 27 of Regulation 2016/1103 sets out, in a positive but non-exhaustive list, the matters that in all cases must fall under the matrimonial property regime. He adds that this provision clearly enshrines a comprehensive regime as well as the principle of the unity of that regime. The concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ within the meaning of that regulation is, by its very design, extremely broad and highly heterogeneous. ( 79 )
72.       Specifically, Article 27(d) of that regulation provides that ‘the powers, rights and obligations of either or both spouses with regard to property’ are to be subject to the law applicable to the matrimonial property regime. Sara Godechot-Patris and Patrick Wautelet ( 80 ) express the view that that provision applies in the case of the acquisition of property in co-ownership, especially where the acquisition is arranged under a contractual separate property regime. I do not share that reservation based on the approach required by Regulation 2016/1103. In the case of a co-ownership arrangement, property relationships between spouses who have opted for the separate property regime, which are not governed by mandatory provisions of the law applicable to the matrimonial property regime, can be governed only by general law. If the fact that that consequence is specific to that regime were not taken into consideration, the scope of that regulation would be limited.
73.       In addition, Article 27(e) of that regulation provides that the law applicable to the matrimonial property regime governs ‘the dissolution of the matrimonial property regime and the partition, distribution or liquidation of the property’.
74.       Some authors argue, on that basis, that Regulation 2016/1103 applies to the division of property between spouses, regardless of whether that division is based on the provisions of a particular matrimonial property regime or more generally on the law of obligations or rights in rem , provided that there is an intrinsic link with the marriage , ( 81 ) and that the organisation of spouses’ property relationships is sufficient, without it being necessary to require a specific regime that necessarily involves a pooling of assets between them. ( 82 )
75.       Consequently, as regards the situation in which the spouses chose a separate property regime when they married, and the two of them solely acquired property together in co-ownership, it may be inferred from Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103, interpreted in conjunction with Article 27 thereof, that the division of that co-ownership arrangement falls within the scope of that regulation and that it should be governed by the law designated by that regulation, whether the division takes place before or after the dissolution of the marriage.
76.       Thirdly, the context of the EU legislature’s objective, which is to give full effect to the principle of the unity of the rules governing couples’ property relationships, ( 83 ) also supports a broad interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’. It must be taken into consideration to a certain extent that Regulation 2016/1103 builds on Regulation No 650/2012. The Court has confirmed that, in most cases, the ‘principle of the unity of jurisdiction and applicable law … informs that regulation’ ( 84 ) and that that principle also underpins the rule established in Article 4 of that regulation, inasmuch as that rule determines the jurisdiction of the courts of the Member States to rule ‘on the succession as a whole’. ( 85 ) However, as some authors point out, ( 86 ) consistency between Regulation No 650/2012 and Regulation 2016/1103 has limitations in practice, since two separate laws may apply, on the one hand, to the couple’s property relationships, and on the other, to succession, because of the different connecting factors provided for by those regulations. In addition, one of the objectives of Regulation No 650/2012, which is to ensure that the court seised applies the law of the forum, is not always achieved in the context of Regulation 2016/1103 because of the principle of the immutability of the applicable law. ( 87 )
77.       Lastly, it is necessary to highlight the specific consequences of that principle of unity for jurisdiction and the applicable law, which support the need for a broad interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ in situations similar to those in the main proceedings. Thus, where spouses who are subject to a separate property regime are co-owners of several immovable properties located in different Member States, and the dispute concerns the liquidation and division of each of those co-owned properties, the fact that Regulation 2016/1103 governs the designation of the competent court and the applicable law is of major importance. ( 88 ) Furthermore, during the liquidation and division of a property held in co-ownership between spouses who are subject to a separate property regime, issues relating to family and property relationships are also likely to arise, which justifies concentrating the resolution of disputes. Such issues may include the settlement of accounts between the spouses, for example where one spouse has financed the property in a proportion different from his or her share as determined at the time of the acquisition of the property, in circumstances arising from their life together as a couple, or the allocation of the family home. ( 89 )
78.       Following the interpretation of the term ‘matrimonial property regime’, as defined in Article 3(1)(a) of Regulation 2016/1103, I am of the view that it must encompass the property relationship between spouses, who are subject to a separate property regime, arising from a co-ownership arrangement between them which is governed by general law.
79.       However, the fact that, in EU law, immovable property is subject to special provisions ( 90 ) makes it necessary to point out that there are certain limitations to be taken into consideration as regards the interpretation of the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’.
D.       Limitations as regards rights in rem
80.       From a methodological point of view, ( 91 ) on account of the exclusions set out in Article 1(2) of Regulation 2016/1103, it is not sufficient, in my view, to find that a co-ownership arrangement between spouses who are subject to a separate property regime falls, in general, within the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’, as defined in that regulation. Depending on the question to be decided by the court seised, it is necessary to ensure that there are no limitations relating to the subject matter of the dispute and the applicable law.
1.       The subject matter of the dispute and the connection with the ‘nature of rights in rem’
81.       In my view, the fact that the dispute concerns a co‑ownership arrangement between (former) spouses does not necessarily mean that it falls within the scope of Regulation 2016/1103, whatever claims may have been made. ( 92 ) Because of the close links between the law on property relationships between spouses and rights in rem , ( 93 ) especially in a dispute of this kind, it is necessary to consider the scope of the exclusion laid down in Article 1(2)(g) of that regulation concerning matters connected with the ‘the nature of rights in rem relating to a property’.
82.       First, it may be noted that, although other regulations treat rights in rem as a ground for exclusive jurisdiction or exclusion, ( 94 ) no definition of that concept is given. ( 95 )
83.       Next, the Court has defined actions which have as their object ‘rights in rem in immovable property’ within the meaning of Article 24(1) of the Brussels I bis Regulation. The Court has held that the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of the Member State in which the property is situated does not encompass all actions concerning rights in rem in immovable property, but only those which both come within the scope of that regulation and are actions which seek to determine the extent, content, ownership or possession of immovable property or the existence of other rights in rem therein and to provide the holders of those rights with protection for the powers which attach to their interest. ( 96 ) The most important criterion is that the powers conferred on them by those rights are effective against third parties. ( 97 )
84.       Lastly, as regards the ‘nature of rights in rem ’, which is also provided for by way of exclusion in Article 1(2)(k) of Regulation No 650/2012, the Court has held that that provision concerns the classification of property and rights and the determination of the prerogatives of the holder of such rights ( 98 ) and that the existence and number of rights in rem in the legal order of the Member States (‘ numerus clausus ’) are covered by the scope of that provision. ( 99 )
85.       In addition, the correlation between the exclusion set out in Article 1(2)(g) of Regulation 2016/1103 and Article 29 of that regulation, ( 100 ) entitled ‘Adaptation of rights in rem ’, confirms that those provisions are intended to guarantee the autonomy of the Member States as regards rights in rem so that they are not required to recognise unknown rights in rem invoked under foreign law.
86.       Accordingly, read in the light of recital 24 of Regulation 2016/1103, the exclusion set out in Article 1(2)(g) of that regulation does not apply where, for example, the issue is whether property acquired jointly by spouses who are subject to a separate property regime is held in co‑ownership between them. ( 101 ) That is also the case for an application, such as that in the main proceedings, which seeks the liquidation and division of co-owned property, in so far as it involves determining the rights of each former spouse under the law applicable to their property relationships. ( 102 ) Moreover, it may be inferred from Article 29 of that regulation, which concerns rights in rem arising from the spouses’ property relationship, that the fact that those rights are governed by provisions other than those of the matrimonial property regime in the strict sense is immaterial. ( 103 ) Finally, the adaptation mechanism laid down in that article justifies examining the function, within the matrimonial property regime, of the right in rem invoked.
87.       I therefore consider that such an analysis of rights in rem is an integral part of defining the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’ as adopted by the EU legislature. It thus appears that the exclusion relating to the ‘nature of rights in rem ’ must be interpreted strictly, on the basis of criteria which do not require the court seised to undertake a level of examination of the application going beyond what is necessary to verify its jurisdiction ab initio .
88.       Moreover, although in the present case other limitations relating to the applicable law do not fall to be applied because of the subject matter of the dispute, I consider that they should nonetheless be highlighted, since they show that certain matters which do not concern ‘the nature of rights in rem ’ nevertheless fall within the scope of the law governing rights in rem and are therefore excluded from the scope of Regulation 2016/1103.
2.       The subject matter of the dispute and the scope of the law governing rights in rem
89.       Several limitations can be identified. Patrick Wautelet explains that the arrangements whereby one of the spouses acquires a right in rem over property are regulated both by the law governing rights in rem and by the law governing the mode of acquisition of that property. ( 104 ) He is also of the view, like other authors, that intervention under the law governing rights in rem could be confined to acts which give concrete effect to the division of the property. ( 105 )
90.       There must also be a further caveat where the implementation of such a division requires a recording in a register. The formalities for such recording are excluded from the scope of Regulation 2016/1103 under Article 1(2)(h) thereof. ( 106 )
91.       After examining the various criteria for assessing the scope of Regulation 2016/1103, I consider, for the purposes of interpreting the concept of a ‘matrimonial property regime’, essentially that:
–        the principle of the unity of jurisdiction and applicable law is defined and given concrete effect by that regulation in order to simplify the organisation of property relationships between (former) spouses, in the light of the particular features of those relationships, which arise from the spouses’ life together;
–        fragmentation of proceedings based on the location of the couple’s property is excluded;
–        the acquisition, in co‑ownership, of property solely by the two spouses, who are subject to a separate property regime, arises from their matrimonial relationship and, a fortiori, from that regime;
–        the fact that general property law is applicable is irrelevant, since it is the only legal framework available to spouses under a separate property regime and its purpose is to organise the property relationship as a result of marriage or its dissolution, or in other words, to govern the spouses’ co‑ownership arrangement. In the present case, in order to resolve the dispute, it may be applied to divide the property between the spouses;
–        the issue of the liquidation and division of immovable property held in co‑ownership by spouses is not covered by the exclusion relating to the ‘nature of rights in rem ’, which has a limited scope; and
–        Article 27(e) of Regulation 2016/ 1103 provides that the law applicable to the matrimonial property regime governs ‘the dissolution of the matrimonial property regime, its liquidation or the division of assets’.
Accordingly, those matters should be dealt with on the basis of Article 27 of Regulation 2016/1103, the law designated in this instance being that chosen by the spouses for their separate property regime.
92.       Finally, in my view, this broadly inclusive approach satisfies the requirement not to complicate, by means of multiple criteria, the court’s determination of its international jurisdiction when it is seised.
93.       Consequently, I propose that the Court answer the referring court’s question in the affirmative, with the result that the court having international jurisdiction would therefore be the court seised in the Czech Republic.
V.       Conclusion
94.       In the light of all the foregoing considerations, I propose that the Court should answer the question referred for a preliminary ruling by the Nejvyšší soud (Supreme Court, Czech Republic) as follows:
The first sentence of Article 1(1) and Article 3(1)(a) of Council Regulation (EU) 2016/1103 implementing enhanced cooperation in the area of jurisdiction, applicable law and the recognition and enforcement of decisions in matters of matrimonial property regimes
must be interpreted as meaning that proceedings for the liquidation and division of immovable property, acquired in co-ownership during marriage by spouses who have opted for a contractual separate property regime, fall within the scope of that regulation.
